lesson.title: Why 2 + 3 * 4 Isn't 20: The Rules Behind the Order
lesson.summary: Operator precedence is the fixed set of rules Python uses to decide which operator runs first when an expression contains more than one, the same logic behind PEMDAS but extended to cover every operator in the language.
lesson.body:
When Python sees an expression like 2 + 3 * 4, it does not simply read left to right the way you might read a sentence. Instead, it consults a ranked list of rules called operator precedence. Multiplication outranks addition, so Python computes 3 * 4 first, getting 12, and only then adds 2, producing 14, not 20. If Python worked left to right with no precedence rules, the same expression would evaluate to 20, which is why this ordering is not a minor detail. It changes the actual answer your program produces.

The hierarchy should feel familiar from math class, since it mirrors PEMDAS. Parentheses are evaluated first because they explicitly override every other rule. Exponentiation, written with **, comes next. Then multiplication, division, floor division, and modulus all share one tier, and within that tier Python works left to right. Addition and subtraction sit at the bottom, also evaluated left to right when they appear together. This is the same ordering the Arithmetic Operators concept introduced for individual operators, except here those operators are competing against each other inside one expression.

Trace a slightly longer example: 2 + 3 * 4 ** 2. Python scans for the highest-precedence operator first, which is **, so it computes 4 ** 2, giving 16. The expression is now effectively 2 + 3 * 16. Multiplication outranks addition, so 3 * 16 happens next, giving 48. Only then does the addition run, 2 + 48, landing on a final value of 50. Each step replaces part of the expression with a single number until one value remains.

This matters beyond passing a quiz question. A common bug looks like average = a + b / 2, written by someone who meant to average two numbers. Because division outranks addition, Python computes b / 2 first and adds a to that result, which is almost never what was intended. The fix is to force the intended order with parentheses: average = (a + b) / 2. Parentheses do not just clarify intent for a human reader, they actually change which computation Python performs, since parentheses sit at the very top of the precedence hierarchy.

A useful habit is to add parentheses even when precedence would already give you the right answer, purely for readability. Writing (x * y) + z instead of x * y + z costs nothing and removes any doubt about what the code does, for you and for anyone reading it later. Precedence rules exist so Python has one unambiguous way to read any expression, but a human reader benefits from not having to run those rules mentally every time. When in doubt about how an expression will evaluate, wrap the part you mean to happen first in parentheses rather than guessing.

One more wrinkle worth knowing about is associativity, which decides what happens when two operators of the same precedence tier sit next to each other. Addition and multiplication associate left to right, so 10 - 3 - 2 evaluates as (10 - 3) - 2, giving 5, not 10 - (3 - 2). Exponentiation is the one common exception, associating right to left instead. That means 2 ** 3 ** 2 evaluates as 2 ** (3 ** 2), computing the inner 3 ** 2 first to get 9, then 2 ** 9, giving 512, rather than computing (2 ** 3) ** 2, which would give a much smaller 64. This right-to-left quirk of ** is easy to forget precisely because every other common operator works left to right, which is exactly why writing out the parentheses explicitly is the safest habit whenever ** appears alongside another operator.
